summary:
The Penal Code in force since November 2012 decriminalised same-sex conduct, and no offence targets consensual activity between adults of the same sex. The sources conflict on the age of consent: two state it is set equally at 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity, while a third states that Law 15/2021 raised it to 18 for everyone in 2021. The higher figure, if correct, applies to visitors as well as residents; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Penal Code Article 130(2)(d) allows enhanced sentencing for crimes motivated by hatred of the victim's sexual orientation. Whether prosecutors have used the provision, and what sentence enhancement results in practice, is not evidenced in the sources.

São Tomé and Príncipe has no legal framework for gender-identity recognition and no procedure for amending sex or gender markers on identity documents. A traveller whose passport, visa or other papers do not match their presentation should expect the mismatch to be visible to border and hotel officials, with no domestic remedy behind it.

No form of relationship recognition exists for same-sex couples: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised, and same-sex couples cannot adopt. Outside the employment context, no general anti-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
São Tomé and Príncipe is listed among the signatories to a joint statement by several governments affirming concerns about sexual orientation and gender identity. The signature is a multilateral position statement and does not itself alter domestic law.

Public attitudes are mixed. A 2016 poll found that 46% of São Toméans would not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour, a figure that leaves substantial social disapproval in view alongside the country's statutory protections.

The pattern in São Tomé and Príncipe matches a wider regional position in which decriminalisation has arrived without recognition, and where protection is confined to employment and sentencing rules rather than a general equality framework. Visitors should not read the presence of those two provisions as evidence of routine safety in daily encounters.
localsOnly:
Labour Code (2019) Article 16.2 bans workplace discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. That provision is the only explicit statutory anti-discrimination protection covering sexual orientation; no general equality law extends the ban to housing, services, education or public life, and gender identity is not named in it.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition. There is no procedure for changing sex or gender markers on national identity documents, so the marker issued at birth or at first registration stands indefinitely.

Same-sex couples cannot marry, cannot register a civil union or domestic partnership, and cannot adopt. Residents in such relationships have no next-of-kin standing, inheritance rights or parental rights derived from the relationship.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources disagree on the age of consent, two giving 16 and one giving 18 from 2021 under Law 15/2021. No consolidating text of the Penal Code or the 2021 statute was available in this inventory to settle the current figure, and no source dated the change in a way that reconciles the two positions.

Not sourced: enforcement data on Penal Code Article 130(2)(d), including whether any prosecution has relied on it; any documented case of violence against a trans person in São Tomé and Príncipe with date and outcome; entry and visa screening practices that could expose a traveller's gender history; availability of gender-affirming healthcare; and rules governing restroom or facility access by gender marker.

Not sourced: whether São Tomé and Príncipe maintains an equality or anti-discrimination body, a hate-crime reporting mechanism, or official guidance for border officials on handling identity documents that do not match a traveller's presentation.
